                                  15             Plaintiff Guangdong Cell Biotechnology Ltd. (“Cell Biotech”) moves to dismiss defendant

                                  16   Thomas Christian Sudhof’s counterclaims on forum non conveniens, international comity, statute

                                  26   alleges that in February 2018, he communicated with three representatives of Cell Biotech to

                                   8          Dr. Sudhof asserts five counterclaims against Cell Biotech: (1) misappropriation of name

                                   9   or likeness in violation of California common law and Cal. Civ. Code § 3344; (2) intentional

                                  10   misrepresentation; (3) negligent misrepresentation; (4) violation of California’s unfair competition

                                  11   law (“UCL”), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200 et seq.; and (5) declaratory relief that Dr. Sudhof

                                  12   “has no contractual obligations to [Cell Biotech] under the alleged MOU and that [Cell Biotech] is
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   not a party entitled to enforce it.” Id. at 9-17. On his own counterclaims, Dr. Sudhof seeks

                                  14   damages, injunctive relief, attorneys’ fees and costs, and pre-judgment and post-judgment interest.

                                  15   Id. at 17-18.

                                  16   II.    LEGAL STANDARD
                                  17          Counterclaims are governed by the same pleading standards that apply to complaints, and

                                  18   likewise, a motion to dismiss a counterclaim is judged according to the standards that apply to a

                                  19   motion to dismiss a claim in a complaint. Strojnik v. Ensemble Hotel Partners, LLC, No. 19-cv-

                                  20   01844-VKD, 2019 WL 5595169, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 30, 2019).

                                  21          A.       Deference to Foreign Forum

                                  22                   1.        Forum non conveniens
                                  23          Forum non conveniens is “an exceptional tool to be employed sparingly.” Ravelo

                                  24   Monegro v. Rosa, 211 F.3d 509, 514 (9th Cir. 2000). Courts considering a motion for dismissal

                                  25   on the ground of forum non conveniens must decide “whether defendants have made a clear

                                  26   showing of facts which establish such oppression and vexation of a defendant as to be out of

                                  27   proportion to plaintiff’s inconvenience . . . .” Boston Telecomms. Grp., Inc. v. Wood, 588 F.3d

                                  28   1201, 1206 (9th Cir. 2009) (quoting Dole Food Co. v. Watts, 303 F.3d 1104, 1118 (9th Cir.
                                                                                         3
                                        Case 5:25-cv-08953-VKD             Document 49          Filed 07/20/26     Page 4 of 23




                                   1   2002)). Defendants face a “heavy burden of proof” in showing that an adequate alternative forum

                                   2   exists where the plaintiff is a United States citizen. Lueck v. Sundstrand Corp., 236 F.3d 1137,

                                   3   1143 (9th Cir. 2001) (citing Piper Aircraft Co. v. Reyno, 454 U.S. 235, 256 (1981)). “Unlike a

                                   4   § 1404(a) motion, a successful motion under forum non conveniens requires dismissal of the case.

                                   5   That inconveniences plaintiffs in several respects and even ‘makes it possible for [plaintiffs] to

                                   6   lose out completely, through the running of the statute of limitations in the forum finally deemed

                                   7   appropriate.” Atl. Marine Constr. Co. v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for W. Dist. of Tex., 571 U.S. 49, 66 n.8

                                   8   (2013) (citations omitted); Carijano v. Occidental Petroleum Corp., 643 F.3d 1216, 1224 (9th Cir.

                                   9   2011) (“The doctrine of forum non conveniens is a drastic exercise of the court’s ‘inherent power’

                                  10   because, unlike a mere transfer of venue, it results in the dismissal of a plaintiff’s case.”).

                                  11            When ruling on a motion to dismiss for forum non conveniens, courts must consider (1) the

                                  12   availability of an adequate alternative forum and (2) whether the balance of private and public
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   interest factors favors dismissal. Lueck, 236 F.3d at 1142 (citing Piper Aircraft, 454 U.S. at 254

                                  14   n.22).

                                  15                   2.      International abstention
                                  16            The doctrine of abstention permits a district court to decline jurisdiction in deference to a

                                  17   parallel proceeding. Colo. River Water Conservation Dist. v. United States, 424 U.S. 800, 813

                                  18   (1976). However, “[a]bstention from the exercise of federal jurisdiction is the exception, not the

                                  19   rule” and applies only in “exceptional circumstances.” Id. The district court should weigh several

                                  20   factors in the international context. These factors include avoidance of piecemeal litigation, the

                                  21   order in which the forums obtained jurisdiction (i.e., the “first-to-file” rule), the rule of decision,

                                  22   parallelism of the suits, avoidance of forum shopping, and appropriate use of judicial resources.

                                  23   See Seneca Ins. Co., Inc. v. Strange Land, Inc., 862 F.3d 835, 841-47 (9th Cir. 2017). These

                                  24   factors are not a checklist; they must instead be considered “with the balance heavily weighted in

                                  25   favor of the exercise of jurisdiction.” Id. at 842 (quoting Moses H. Cone Mem’l Hosp. v. Mercury

                                  26   Constr. Corp., 460 U.S. 1, 16 (1983)). “Though ‘exact parallelism . . . is not required,’ substantial

                                  27   similarity of claims is necessary before abstention is available.” Id. at 845 (quoting Nakash v.

                                  28   Marciano, 882 F.2d 1411, 1416 (9th Cir. 1989)). Still, “conflicting results, piecemeal litigation,
                                                                                           4
                                        Case 5:25-cv-08953-VKD            Document 49          Filed 07/20/26     Page 5 of 23




                                   1   and some duplication of judicial effort is the unavoidable price of preserving access to . . . federal

                                   2   relief.” Tovar v. Billmeyer, 609 F.2d 1291, 1293 (9th Cir. 1979). The Ninth Circuit “reject[s] the

                                   3   notion that a federal court owes greater deference to foreign courts than to our own state courts.”

                                   4   Neuchatel Swiss Gen. Ins. Co. v. Lufthansa Airlines, 925 F.2d 1193, 1195 (9th Cir. 1991).

                                   5                  3.      International comity
                                   6           “International comity is a doctrine of prudential abstention, one that counsels voluntary

                                   7   forbearance when a sovereign which has a legitimate claim to jurisdiction concludes that a second

                                   8   sovereign also has a legitimate claim to jurisdiction under principles of international law.” Mujica

                                   9   v. AirScan Inc., 771 F.3d 580, 598 (9th Cir. 2014) (quotation marks and citation omitted). The

                                  10   aspect of the doctrine referred to as “comity among courts” or “adjudicatory comity,” is “viewed

                                  11   as a discretionary act of deference by a national court to decline to exercise jurisdiction in a case

                                  12   properly adjudicated in a foreign state.” Id. at 599 (quotation marks and citation omitted).
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   “[C]ourts have struggled to apply a consistent set of factors in their comity analyses.” Id. at 603.

                                  14           The Ninth Circuit has found the following factors to be a useful starting point: (1) “the

                                  15   strength of the United States’ interest in using a foreign forum”; (2) “the strength of the foreign

                                  16   governments’ interests”; and (3) “the adequacy of the alternative forum.” Id. (quotation marks and

                                  17   citation omitted). With respect to the first factor, U.S. interests, the Ninth Circuit has articulated a

                                  18   non-exclusive list of considerations, including: “(1) the location of the conduct in question, (2) the

                                  19   nationality of the parties, (3) the character of the conduct in question, (4) the foreign policy

                                  20   interests of the United States, and (5) any public policy interests.” Id. at 604. With respect to the

                                  21   second factor, foreign interests, the Ninth Circuit has held that “[t]he proper analysis of foreign

                                  22   interests essentially mirrors the consideration of U.S. interests.” Id. at 607. Finally, with respect

                                  23   to the third factor, adequacy of the alternative forum, the Court considers whether the plaintiff has

                                  24   shown that the alternative forum is “clearly unsatisfactory” or would result in “manifest injustice.”

                                  25   Id. at 614.

                                  26           B.     Rule 9(b)
                                  27           Allegations sounding in fraud, including allegations of false advertising, are subject to the

                                  28   heightened pleading standard under Rule 9(b). Clorox Co. v. Reckitt Benckiser Grp. PLC, 398 F.
                                                                                          5
                                        Case 5:25-cv-08953-VKD            Document 49          Filed 07/20/26     Page 6 of 23




                                   1   Supp. 3d 623, 634 (N.D. Cal. 2019) (stating that UCL claims sounding in fraud are subject to the

                                   2   Rule 9(b) standard). Under Rule 9(b), allegations of fraud must be pled “with particularity.” Fed.

                                   3   R. Civ. P. 9(b). However, “[m]alice, intent, knowledge, and other conditions of a person’s mind

                                   4   may be alleged generally.” Id. “A pleading is sufficient under Rule 9(b) if it identifies the

                                   5   circumstances constituting fraud so that the defendant can prepare an adequate answer from the

                                   6   allegations.” Neubronner v. Milken, 6 F.3d 666, 671-72 (9th Cir. 1993) (citations and quotations

                                   7   omitted). This includes pleading “the who, what, when, where, and how of the misconduct

                                   8   charged.” Whiteside v. Kimberly Clark Corp., 108 F.4th 771, 785 (9th Cir. 2024) (citation and

                                   9   quotations omitted).

                                  10          C.      Rule 12(b)(6)
                                  11          A motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6) tests the legal

                                  12   sufficiency of the claims in the complaint. Navarro v. Block, 250 F.3d 729, 732 (9th Cir. 2001).
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Dismissal is appropriate where there is no cognizable legal theory or an absence of sufficient facts

                                  14   alleged to support a cognizable legal theory. Id. (citing Balistreri v. Pacifica Police Dep’t, 901

                                  15   F.2d 696, 699 (9th Cir. 1990)). On such a motion, all material allegations in the complaint must

                                  16   be taken as true and construed in the light most favorable to the claimant. Id.

                                  17          A complaint should be dismissed for failure to state a claim if it fails to set forth “enough

                                  18   facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.” Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S.

                                  19   544, 570 (2007); see also Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6). “Threadbare recitals of the elements of a cause

                                  20   of action, supported by mere conclusory statements, do not suffice,” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S.

                                  21   662, 678 (2009), and “[f]actual allegations must be enough to raise a right to relief above the

                                  22   speculative level,” Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555 (citations omitted). Moreover, the Court is not

                                  23   required to “‘assume the truth of legal conclusions merely because they are cast in the form of

                                  24   factual allegations.’” Prager Univ. v. Google LLC, No. 17-cv-06064-LHK, 2018 WL 1471939, at

                                  25   *3 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 26, 2018) (quoting Fayer v. Vaughn, 649 F.3d 1061, 1064 (9th Cir. 2011) (per

                                  26   curiam)). Nor does the Court accept allegations that contradict documents attached to the

                                  27   complaint or incorporated by reference, Gonzalez v. Planned Parenthood of L.A., 759 F.3d 1112,

                                  28   1115 (9th Cir. 2014), or that rest on “allegations that are merely conclusory, unwarranted
                                                                                          6
                                        Case 5:25-cv-08953-VKD            Document 49          Filed 07/20/26     Page 7 of 23




                                   1   deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences,” In re Gilead Scis. Sec. Litig., 536 F.3d 1049, 1055

                                   2   (9th Cir. 2008).

                                   3          D.      Rule 12(f)
                                   4          Before responding to a pleading, a party may move to strike any “redundant, immaterial,

                                   5   impertinent or scandalous matter.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(f). A matter is “immaterial” if it “has no

                                   6   essential or important relationship to the claim for relief or the defenses being pleaded.” Fantasy,

                                   7   Inc. v. Fogerty, 984 F.2d 1524, 1527 (9th Cir. 1993), rev’d on other grounds, 510 U.S. 517 (1994)

                                   8   (internal quotation marks omitted). A matter is “impertinent” if it “do[es] not pertain, and [is] not

                                   9   necessary, to the issues in question.” Id. (internal quotation marks omitted). “Scandalous”

                                  10   allegations include those that “cast a cruelly derogatory light on a party or other person.” Figy v.

                                  11   Lifeway Foods, Inc., No. 13-cv-04828-TEH, 2016 WL 4364225, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 16, 2016).

                                  12          “[T]he function of a [Rule] 12(f) motion to strike is to avoid the expenditure of time and
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   money that must arise from litigating spurious issues by dispensing with those issues prior to trial .

                                  14   . . .” Sidney-Vinstein v. A.H. Robins Co., 697 F.2d 880, 885 (9th Cir. 1983). Motions to strike are

                                  15   generally disfavored and “should not be granted unless the matter to be stricken clearly could have

                                  16   no possible bearing on the subject of the litigation.” Platte Anchor Bolt, Inc. v. IHI, Inc., 352 F.

                                  17   Supp. 2d 1048, 1057 (N.D. Cal. 2004). “A court must deny the motion to strike if there is any

                                  18   doubt whether the allegations in the pleadings might be relevant in the action.” Oracle Am., Inc. v.

                                  19   Micron Tech., Inc., 817 F. Supp. 2d 1128, 1132 (N.D. Cal. 2011). When ruling on a motion to

                                  20   strike, the Court must accept the nonmoving party’s allegations as true and liberally construe the

                                  21   attacked pleading in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party. Stearns v. Select Comfort

                                  22   Retail Corp., 763 F. Supp. 2d 1128, 1140 (N.D. Cal. 2010).

                                  23   III.   MOTION TO DISMISS

                                  24          Cell Biotech moves to dismiss all counterclaims on forum non conveniens, international

                                  25   abstention, and international comity grounds. Dkt. No. 33 at 16-24. Cell Biotech also moves to

                                  26   dismiss the first counterclaim on statute of limitations grounds and the second, third, fourth, and

                                  27   fifth counterclaims for failure to state a claim for relief. Id. at 4-16. Cell Biotech also requests

                                  28   judicial notice of five documents. Dkt. No. 33-2. The Court first addresses Cell Biotech’s request
                                                                                          7
                                        Case 5:25-cv-08953-VKD            Document 49           Filed 07/20/26    Page 8 of 23




                                   1   for judicial notice. Then, the Court addresses Cell Biotech’s forum non conveniens argument

                                   2   before addressing its other arguments for dismissal. See Sinochem Int’l Co. v. Malaysia Int’l

                                   3   Shipping Corp., 549 U.S. 422, 425 (2007) (“[A] district court has discretion to respond at once to

                                   4   a defendant’s forum non conveniens plea, and need not take up first any other threshold

                                   5   objection.”).

                                   6          A.       Cell Biotech’s Request for Judicial Notice
                                   7          In connection with its motion to dismiss, Cell Biotech asks the Court to take judicial notice

                                   8   of five documents from another judicial proceeding between the same parties in China (“China

                                   9   Proceeding”): (1) the parties’ MOU, dated March 9, 2018; (2) Dr. Sudhof’s civil complaint filed in

                                  10   the China Proceeding; (3) an English translation of Dr. Sudhof’s complaint in the China

                                  11   Proceeding; (4) excerpts from the evidentiary materials submitted by Dr. Sudhof in the China

                                  12   Proceeding; and (5) an English translation of the excerpts from the evidentiary materials submitted
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   by Dr. Sudhof in the China Proceeding. Dkt. No. 33-2 at 2-3, Exs. A-E. Dr. Sudhof opposes Cell

                                  14   Biotech’s request for judicial notice on the grounds that the accuracy of the documents is

                                  15   questionable; the English translations cannot readily be verified; and the Chinese court documents

                                  16   are not materials “within the trial court’s territorial jurisdiction.” Dkt. No. 37 at 8-9.

                                  17          Federal Rule of Evidence 201 provides that “[t]he court may judicially notice a fact that is

                                  18   not subject to reasonable dispute because it . . . can be accurately and readily determined from

                                  19   sources whose accuracy cannot reasonably be questioned.” Fed. R. Evid. 201(b)(2); see also

                                  20   Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc., 899 F.3d 988, 999 (9th Cir. 2018). These reliable sources

                                  21   include “matters of public record . . . as long as the facts noticed are not subject to reasonable

                                  22   dispute.” Intri-Plex Techs., Inc. v. Crest Grp., Inc., 499 F.3d 1048, 1052 (9th Cir. 2007) (cleaned

                                  23   up). Accordingly, while a court may take judicial notice of matters of public record when

                                  24   deciding a motion to dismiss, it “cannot take judicial notice of disputed facts contained in such

                                  25   public records.” Khoja, 899 F.3d at 999.

                                  26          “In a motion to dismiss for forum non conveniens, the allegations in the complaint need

                                  27   not be accepted as true, and the court may consider evidence outside the pleadings.” Dickens v.

                                  28   NXP Semiconductors, 703 F. Supp. 3d 1013, 1019 (N.D. Cal. 2023) (quoting Farhang v. Indian
                                                                                           8
                                        Case 5:25-cv-08953-VKD            Document 49          Filed 07/20/26    Page 9 of 23




                                   1   Inst. of Tech., No. 08-cv-02658-RMW, 2012 WL 113739, at *8 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 12, 2012)).

                                   2          Dr. Sudhof admits that he initiated the China Proceeding on November 5, 2024 and that the

                                   3   parties recently completed a trial in the China Proceeding. Dkt. No. 37 at 6-7. Dr. Sudhof himself

                                   4   previously filed a copy of his complaint from the China Proceeding and an English translation of

                                   5   that complaint in the instant case in connection with his motion to dismiss Cell Biotech’s

                                   6   complaint. Dkt. No. 5-1 ¶¶ 2-3, Exs. A-B. Dr. Sudhof’s and Cell Biotech’s English translations

                                   7   of the complaint filed in the China Proceeding are not identical, but the crux of that complaint is

                                   8   that Cell Biotech allegedly infringed Dr. Sudhof’s “portrait and name rights via the internet.”

                                   9   Compare Dkt. No. 5-1 ¶ 3, Ex. B with Dkt. No. 33-2 at 2, Ex. C.

                                  10          The Court takes judicial notice of the complaint filed in the China Proceeding and the

                                  11   English translation of that complaint filed by Dr. Sudhof at Dkt. No. 5-1 ¶¶ 2-3, Exs. A-B. The

                                  12   Court takes judicial notice of these documents solely for the purpose of noticing the existence of
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   the China Proceeding and the nature of Dr. Sudhof’s claims in the China Proceeding, so that the

                                  14   Court may properly evaluate Cell Biotech’s forum non conveniens arguments. See Aldini AG v.

                                  26              Accordingly, the Court dismisses Dr. Sudhof’s intentional misrepresentation counterclaim

                                  27   under Rules 9(b) and 12(b)(6), with leave to amend.

                                  28
                                                                                           19

                                   1                  2.      Negligent misrepresentation (third counterclaim)

                                   2          Cell Biotech moves to dismiss Dr. Sudhof’s counterclaim for negligent misrepresentation

                                   3   pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6). Dkt. No. 33 at 10-12. Specifically, Cell Biotech contends that the

                                   4   alleged misrepresentations are non-actionable “promises of future conduct.” Id. at 11. Dr. Sudhof

                                   5   did not respond to Cell Biotech’s specific arguments regarding the third counterclaim. See Dkt.

                                   6   No. 37 at 10-13.

                                   7          Under California law, the elements of a claim for negligent misrepresentation are: “(1) a

                                   8   misrepresentation of a past or existing material fact, (2) made without reasonable ground for

                                   9   believing it to be true, (3) made with the intent to induce another’s reliance on the fact

                                  10   misrepresented, (4) justifiable reliance on the misrepresentation, and (5) resulting damage.” Alafi

                                  11   v. Cohen, 106 Cal. App. 5th 46, 65 (Cal. Ct. App. 2024) (quoting Ragland v. U.S. Nat’l Bank

                                  12   Ass’n, 209 Cal. App. 4th 182, 196 (Cal. Ct. App. 2012)). A negligent misrepresentation must
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   pertain to a past or existing fact; predictions of future events or actions are not actionable. See,

                                  14   e.g., Romo v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., No. 15-cv-03708-EMC, 2016 WL 324286, at *11 (N.D.

                                  15   Cal. Jan. 27, 2016).

                                  16          Here, Cell Biotech’s statements, as alleged in the counterclaim, could be construed not as

                                  17   predictions as to future events, but as representations that Cell Biotech would establish a

                                  18   laboratory. In Rufini v. CitiMortage, Inc., the court held that allegations that the defendant stated

                                  19   that the plaintiff was approved for a loan modification and that he would receive a permanent

                                  20   modification in the near future were “sufficient, for purposes of demurrer, to state a claim for

                                  21   negligent misrepresentation.” 227 Cal. App. 4th 299, 302, 308 (Cal. Ct. App. 2014). Similarly,

                                  22   here, the counterclaim plausibly alleges that Cell Biotech’s statement that it would build a

                                  23   laboratory was a misrepresentation of an existing fact. See Nido v. Nationwide Mut. Ins. Co., No.

                                  24   19-cv-07724-LHK, 2020 WL 1865324, at *7 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 14, 2020) (finding that it was “not

                                  25   obvious according to the settled rules of California that [p]laintiffs could not prevail on their

                                  26   negligent misrepresentation claim” where plaintiffs alleged that an insurance company’s

                                  27   representative stated that the insurance company would approve their construction contract and

                                  28   reimburse them).
                                                                                         20

                                   1          However, Dr. Sudhof fails to plead any non-conclusory allegations about causation and

                                   2   harm. As with the intentional misrepresentation counterclaim, Dr. Sudhof states that Cell

                                   3   Biotech’s negligent misrepresentations “have harmed, and are the substantial factor in causing the

                                   4   harm to Dr. Sudhof’s ability to enter into certain business relationship sand prospective economic

                                   5   engagements.” Dkt. No. 31 at 15. This is insufficient to state a claim for negligent

                                   6   misrepresentation.

                                   7          The Court grants the motion to dismiss the negligent misrepresentation claim under Rule

                                   8   12(b)(6), with leave to amend.

                                   9                  3.      UCL (fourth counterclaim)
                                  10          Dr. Sudhof alleges that Cell Biotech engaged in “an unlawful and unfair business act when

                                  11   it misappropriated Dr. Sudhof’s name and likeness on its website” and “also engaged in an

                                  12   unlawful, unfair, and fraudulent business act when it induced Dr. Sudhof to enter into the MOU
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   via intentional misrepresentations.” Dkt. No. 31 at 16.

                                  14          The UCL prohibits “any unlawful, unfair or fraudulent business act or practice and unfair,

                                  15   deceptive, untrue or misleading advertising.” Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200. The California

                                  16   Supreme Court has clarified that the UCL, because it is “written in the disjunctive,” prohibits three

                                  17   separate types of unfair competition: (1) unlawful acts or practices, (2) unfair acts or practices, and

                                  18   (3) fraudulent acts or practices. Cel-Tech Commc’ns, Inc. v. Los Angeles Cellular Tel. Co., 20

                                  19   Cal. 4th 163, 180 (Cal. 1999); accord Davis v. HSBC Bank Nev., N.A., 691 F.3d 1152, 1168 (9th

                                  20   Cir. 2012). To plead a UCL claim, a plaintiff's allegations must show that a defendant’s conduct

                                  21   violates one of these three “prongs.” Id. Dr. Sudhof asserts a UCL claim under all three prongs.

                                  22          Cell Biotech argues Dr. Sudhof’s fourth counterclaim should be dismissed because it

                                  23   simply incorporates and repeats the same allegations underlying the first counterclaim for

                                  24   misappropriation and second counterclaim for intentional misrepresentation. Dkt. No. 33 at 13.

                                  25   Cell Biotech contends the UCL claim “does not identify any distinct conduct, any separate injury,

                                  26   or any independent basis for relief.” Id. Dr. Sudhof responds that even if the fourth counterclaim

                                  27   is duplicative of the first and second counterclaims, he is permitted to plead “alternative theories

                                  28   of recovery.” Dkt. No. 37 at 13. He further argues that because UCL claims “borrow” violations
                                                                                         21
                                        Case 5:25-cv-08953-VKD           Document 49       Filed 07/20/26      Page 22 of 23




                                   1   from other laws, it follows that the fourth counterclaim will be brought with regard to the same

                                   2   conduct as other counterclaims. Id. Dr. Sudhof argues that the fourth counterclaim adequately

                                   3   states a claim for relief because the alleged misconduct is “precisely the type of conduct

                                   4   proscribed by the UCL, even if it is the same conduct underlying other Counterclaims.” Id. at 14.

                                   5          At the hearing, Dr. Sudhof conceded that the fourth counterclaim rises and falls with the

                                   6   first, second, and third counterclaims. Dkt. No. 46. As the Court has dismissed the first, second,

                                   7   and third counterclaims, the Court also grants the motion to dismiss the fourth counterclaim, with

                                   8   leave to amend.

                                   9                  4.      Declaratory relief (fifth counterclaim)
                                  10          Cell Biotech moves to dismiss the fifth counterclaim on the basis that it is “entirely

                                  11   duplicative of the issues already presented by the Complaint.” Dkt. No. 33 at 14-16. Dr. Sudhof

                                  12   responds that the counterclaim is not duplicative because he seeks “additional and different relief,”
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   specifically, “a declaration that the MOU is not valid, not binding, not enforceable, and that [Cell

                                  14   Biotech] is itself not a party to the MOU.” Dkt. No. 37 at 15.

                                  15          “Federal courts do not have a duty to grant declaratory judgment; therefore, it is within a

                                  16   district court’s discretion to dismiss an action for declaratory judgment.” Leadsinger, Inc. v. BMG

                                  17   Music Pub., 512 F.3d 522, 533 (9th Cir. 2008). “District courts have dismissed counterclaims

                                  18   under the Declaratory Judgment Act where they have found them to be repetitious of issues

                                  19   already before the court via the complaint or affirmative defenses.” Stickrath v. Globalstar, Inc.,

                                  20   No. 07-cv-1941 TEH, 2008 WL 2050990, at *3 (N.D. Cal. May 13, 2008) (citation omitted).

                                  21          Here, there is “perfect symmetry” between the issue presented in Cell Biotech’s operative

                                  22   complaint and the issue raised in Dr. Sudhof’s fifth counterclaim. See CBS Outdoor LLC v. Cal.

                                  23   Mini Storage, LLC, No. 14-cv-01598 SI, 2014 WL 5282088, at *7 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 15, 2014)

                                  24   (granting Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss defendants’ counterclaim for declaratory relief). The

                                  25   adjudication of Cell Biotech’s breach of contract claim “will necessarily moot” any need for the

                                  26   declaratory relief that Dr. Sudhof seeks. See id.; see also Berger v. Seyfarth Shaw, LLP, No. 07-

                                  27   cv-05279 JSW, 2008 WL 2468478, at *2 (N.D. Cal. June 17, 2008) (dismissing declaratory

                                  28   judgment counterclaims because there was “nothing before the Court to suggest that Defendants’
                                                                                        22
                                        Case 5:25-cv-08953-VKD           Document 49         Filed 07/20/26      Page 23 of 23




                                   1   declaratory judgment counterclaims would entitle them to any costs or fees beyond those it might

                                   2   otherwise be entitled to as a result of successfully defending against Plaintiffs’ suit”).

                                   3           Accordingly, the Court grants Cell Biotech’s motion to dismiss the fifth counterclaim,

                                   4   without leave to amend.

                                   5   IV.     MOTION TO STRIKE

                                   6           Cell Biotech asks the Court to strike the fifth counterclaim as redundant of Cell Biotech’s

                                   7   complaint. Dkt. No. 34. This is the same argument Cell Biotech raised in its Rule 12(b)(6)

                                   8   motion to dismiss the fifth counterclaim. Compare id. with Dkt. No. 33 at 14-16.

                                   9           As the Court has already granted Cell Biotech’s Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss the fifth

                                  10   counterclaim, the Court denies Cell Biotech’s Rule 12(f) motion to strike the fifth counterclaim as

                                  11   moot.

                                  12   V.      CONCLUSION
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13           For the reasons explained above, the Court denies Cell Biotech’s motion to strike as moot,

                                  14   and grants Cell Biotech’s motion to dismiss, as follows:

                                  15           (1) Counterclaim 1 (misappropriation of name or likeness) is dismissed, with leave to

                                  16              amend, only as to allegations of new misappropriation, if any, not at issue in the China

                                  17              Proceeding.

                                  18           (2) Counterclaim 2 (intentional misrepresentation) is dismissed, with leave to amend.

                                  19           (3) Counterclaim 3 (negligent misrepresentation) is dismissed, with leave to amend.

                                  20           (4) Counterclaim 4 (UCL) is dismissed, with leave to amend.

                                  21           (5) Counterclaim 5 (declaratory relief) is dismissed, without leave to amend.

                                  22           Dr. Sudhof may file an amended counterclaim no later than August 3, 2026.
